title: One Year On: The Night India's Women Won the World Cup and Changed the Game
excerpt: On November 2, 2025, India beat South Africa by 52 runs in Navi Mumbai for a first ICC title. A year later, the endorsements have transformed — the T20 crown is still missing.
body:
• On November 2, 2025, India beat South Africa by 52 runs at DY Patil Stadium, Navi Mumbai, to win their first Women's ODI World Cup — a year ago on Monday, and still the night that changed the economics of the women's game in India.
  • Shafali Verma, a late injury replacement who was not in the original squad, made 87 and took 2 wickets in the final; Deepti Sharma made 58 and took five wickets.
  • Endorsement values for leading players surged 25 to 100% after the win, according to industry estimates reported by The Economic Times and cited by India Today.
  • A year on, the unfinished business is T20 cricket: India failed to reach the 2026 Women's T20 World Cup semi-finals, and coach Amol Muzumdar is building toward dominance rather than declaring it.

A year ago on Monday, the match ran past midnight and a country stayed up for it. On November 2, 2025, India beat South Africa by 52 runs in the Women's ODI World Cup final at DY Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai to win their first ICC title, ending a run of final defeats that included the 2017 ODI World Cup and the 2020 T20 World Cup. India Today's anniversary account calls it, simply, the night Indian women's cricket found its wings.

A final won by the unlikely names

The final's central figure was not supposed to be there. Shafali Verma was not in India's original World Cup squad, carried an ODI average of 22 and had not made a half-century in more than three years. Drafted in only after Pratika Rawal's injury — Rawal, injured, celebrated the win in a wheelchair — Shafali made 87 in the final to set up India's 298 for 7, then took two wickets, including Marizanne Kapp.

Deepti Sharma's final was a redemption arc inside the match: criticised for slow scoring during the group defeats, she made a crucial 58 and then took a five-wicket haul. South Africa captain Laura Wolvaardt, who had made 169 in the semi-final, scored 101 in the final — and her dismissal, a juggled catch finally held by Amanjot Kaur off Deepti, was the moment the result settled. Captain Harmanpreet Kaur took the final catch, of Nadine de Klerk, to close the match.

"This is just the beginning. We wanted to break this barrier, and now we've done it. Our next goal is to make this consistent."

— Harmanpreet Kaur, after the final, reported by Circle of Cricket

The campaign nearly ended early

The anniversary framing can make the win sound inevitable. It was not. India lost three group matches in a row — to Australia, South Africa and England — and their 330-plus total against Australia was chased down. A commanding win over New Zealand restored them, and in the semi-final they chased 339 against Australia, then the highest successful chase in women's ODIs, behind Jemimah Rodrigues' unbeaten 127. The final was against the South Africa side that had beaten them in the group stage, as Circle of Cricket's contemporary report recorded.

What changed in a year

The commercial shift is the measurable part. India Today, citing industry estimates reported by The Economic Times in November 2025, put the post-title surge in endorsement values for leading players at 25 to 100%: Rodrigues from around Rs 60 lakh to over Rs 1.5 crore, Shafali from around Rs 40 lakh to more than Rs 1 crore, with Harleen Deol landing a skincare endorsement and players entering automobile, banking, fintech and consumer-technology campaigns once reserved for male stars.

The cricketing shift is incomplete. India failed to reach the semi-finals of the 2026 Women's T20 World Cup, losing the decisive group match to Australia, who won their seventh title. Head coach Amol Muzumdar has said he would be happy if India began dominating world cricket two years down the line. That, a year after the night in Navi Mumbai, is the right note to end the anniversary on: the barrier Harmanpreet described is broken; the dynasty is not yet built.
